body:
India's challenge after Independence

When India became independent in 1947, its leaders had to unite territories that differed in language, culture and administrative history. British provincial boundaries had not always followed linguistic divisions. Some regions had been directly administered by the British, while others had belonged to princely states.

One important question was whether people speaking a common regional language should have a state of their own within the Indian Union. Such a state would allow regional languages to have a greater role in administration and public life. However, the experience of Partition made national leaders cautious about changing boundaries immediately.

Linguistic reorganisation means redrawing state boundaries with language as an important consideration. It does not mean creating an independent country or separating a region from the Indian Union.

The movement towards linguistic states

The Indian National Congress had recognised the linguistic principle in organising its provincial committees during the freedom struggle. After Independence, demands for linguistic states became stronger, especially in Telugu-speaking areas of the former Madras State.

The death of Potti Sriramulu during a fast demanding a separate Andhra State intensified public protests. Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953. The Union government also appointed the States Reorganisation Commission in 1953 to examine the wider question of state boundaries.

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 substantially redrew India's internal boundaries. Nevertheless, every linguistic demand was not settled in 1956. One important exception was the enlarged bilingual Bombay State, which contained substantial Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking populations.

Why Bombay State became a special issue

The 1956 reorganisation brought the former Saurashtra and Kutch regions into the enlarged Bombay State along with other territories. Gujarati-speaking areas therefore shared a state administration with Marathi-speaking areas. This arrangement did not satisfy those who wanted separate states reflecting the two major linguistic communities.

The subsequent agitation led to the division of Bombay State in 1960. Gujarat formally came into existence on 1 May 1960, and its public inauguration took place at Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad.

Prelims focus

  • Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
  • The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in 1953.
  • The States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956.
  • The enlarged Bombay State was bilingual, with major Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking populations.
  • Gujarat was formed on 1 May 1960.
  • Trap: The 1956 Act reorganised Bombay State; it did not create Gujarat as a separate state.

[NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, Chapter 10, 'India After Independence,' printed pp. 133–135, 2020–21 printing; NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, 'Challenges of Nation Building,' printed pp. 19–23; Gujarat Legislative Assembly, 'Historical Background,' National e-Vidhan Application legislative information; Hindustan Times, 'From HT Archives: Maharashtra and Gujarat Born Anew as States of Union,' archival account republished 4 May 2024, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Citizens in period clothing gather beneath a neem tree in Sabarmati Ashram’s courtyard to commemorate Gujarat’s formation in 1960.
A timeline distinguishes the 1953 developments, the enlarged bilingual Bombay State in 1956, and separate Gujarat formed on 1 May 1960.

title: From Independence to the Demand for a Gujarati-Speaking State

body:
Meaning and objective of Mahagujarat

The Mahagujarat Movement was the political and popular movement demanding a separate state for Gujarati-speaking people. Its central objective was to end the bilingual Bombay arrangement and bring the Gujarati-speaking regions together under a state government of their own.

The name Mahagujarat expressed the idea of a larger, united Gujarati-speaking region. This included the mainland Gujarati-speaking districts as well as Saurashtra and Kutch, which had previously experienced different administrative arrangements.

The demand was for a separate state within India, not for independence from India. This distinction is essential because the movement was part of the wider history of linguistic reorganisation in the Indian Union.

Indulal Yagnik and the Mahagujarat Janata Parishad

Indulal Kanaiyalal Yagnik was the best-known leader of the Mahagujarat Movement. He was popularly known as Induchacha. He became closely associated with the campaign for a separate Gujarati-speaking state.

The Mahagujarat Janata Parishad was formed in 1956 and played an important organisational role in the demand. It brought the separate-state question into political debate and electoral mobilisation. Indulal Yagnik served as its president.

The movement combined a demand based on language with dissatisfaction over the continued existence of bilingual Bombay State. It developed through public meetings, demonstrations and political activity rather than through a single government decision.

The parallel demand in Maharashtra

At the same time, the Samyukta Maharashtra Movement sought a state for Marathi-speaking people. The two movements arose from the same administrative problem but represented different linguistic demands.

MovementMain demandAssociated region
MahagujaratSeparate Gujarati-speaking stateGujarat, including Saurashtra and Kutch
Samyukta MaharashtraSeparate Marathi-speaking stateMarathi-speaking territories of Bombay State

The position of Bombay city was an important point of contention. The Mahagujarat Janata Parishad's stated demand included Bombay city, but the final reorganisation placed the city in Maharashtra. Therefore, the geographical claims made during a movement should not automatically be treated as the boundaries established by the final law.

The political settlement of 1960

Prolonged agitation and political negotiation resulted in the decision to divide bilingual Bombay State. The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 provided the legal basis for the change. On 1 May 1960, Gujarat and Maharashtra began functioning as separate states.

In this way, the movement illustrates how a regional demand could lead to a constitutional change without breaking national unity. Linguistic identity became a basis for state administration while both successor states remained parts of India.

Prelims focus

  • Indulal K. Yagnik was the leading figure of the Mahagujarat Movement.
  • The Mahagujarat Janata Parishad was formed in 1956.
  • Mahagujarat demanded a separate state for Gujarati-speaking people.
  • Samyukta Maharashtra demanded a separate state for Marathi-speaking people.
  • The final 1960 settlement placed Bombay city in Maharashtra.
  • Trap: Do not confuse the Mahagujarat Movement with the Navnirman Movement of 1974.

[The Nehru Archive, 'Mahagujerat Janata Parishad,' organisation record, consulted 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, 'Challenges of Nation Building,' printed pp. 21–23; Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, section 3, India Code; Times of India, 'Movements That Shaped Davids and Goliaths of Gujarat Politics,' 27 November 2022, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Mahagujarat and Samyukta Maharashtra sought linguistic states; Bombay city appeared in the Parishad's claim but joined Maharashtra on 1 May 1960.
pictures.caption: The final legal boundary need not include every territory claimed during an agitation.

title: The Mahagujarat Movement: Leadership, Demands and Outcome

body:
The law that created Gujarat

The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 was enacted by the Parliament of India as Act 11 of 1960. It is dated 25 April 1960. Section 2(a) defines the Act's appointed day as 1 May 1960.

The distinction between these dates is important. The date of an Act and the date on which a particular legal change takes effect need not be the same. Gujarat's statehood began on the appointed day, not on 25 April.

Formation date: 1 May 1960.
Governing law: Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.
Relevant provision: Section 3, read with the appointed-day definition in Section 2(a).

How Bombay State was divided

Section 3 formed a new state named Gujarat from specified territories of the former Bombay State. These included 17 named districts and certain specified villages. The named districts covered the mainland Gujarati region as well as Saurashtra and Kutch.

The remainder of Bombay State was legally designated the State of Maharashtra. Thus, the Act created Gujarat from transferred territories and renamed the residuary Bombay State as Maharashtra.

Both states remained within the Indian Union. This was a change to internal state boundaries under the constitutional framework, not a division of India into separate countries.

The first Legislative Assembly

The new state required its own legislature. The Act provided for members representing the transferred Gujarat constituencies in the Bombay Legislative Assembly to become members of the Gujarat Legislative Assembly.

At formation, the Gujarat Assembly had 132 members. Its strength subsequently increased to 154 in 1962, 168 in 1967 and 182 in 1975. These are different historical membership figures; the number at the time of formation should not be confused with the later figure.

The High Court and the first state leadership

Section 28 of the Act established a separate High Court of Gujarat from 1 May 1960. It began functioning in Ahmedabad, taking over jurisdiction relating to the territories of the new state from the Bombay High Court. Justice Sunderlal Trikamlal Desai was its first Chief Justice.

Dr. Jivraj Narayan Mehta became Gujarat's first Chief Minister. Mehdi Nawaz Jung became its first Governor. These were different constitutional offices: the Chief Minister headed the elected state government, whereas the Governor was the constitutional head of the state.

The formal public inauguration of Gujarat took place at Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad on 1 May 1960, with Ravishankar Maharaj associated with the inauguration ceremony. The ceremony marked the beginning of the new state; its legal creation followed from the parliamentary Act.

Prelims focus

  • Bombay Reorganisation Act: Act 11 of 1960, dated 25 April 1960.
  • Section 2(a): appointed day of 1 May 1960.
  • Section 3: formation of Gujarat from specified Bombay State territories.
  • Gujarat's first Assembly had 132 members.
  • Section 28: separate Gujarat High Court from 1 May 1960.
  • First Chief Minister: Dr. Jivraj Narayan Mehta; first Governor: Mehdi Nawaz Jung.
  • Trap: The Act's date, 25 April 1960, is not Gujarat's formation date.

[Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, Act 11 of 1960, sections 2(a), 3, 13, 15, 19 and 28, India Code; Gujarat Legislative Assembly, 'Historical Background,' National e-Vidhan Application legislative information; Gujarat High Court, official 'About Gujarat High Court' page, consulted 23 November 2026; Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Second Series, Volume 59, p. 202, 'Message: Formation of Gujarat,' 13 April 1960; Volume 60, p. 339, letter to President Rajendra Prasad, 23 April 1960, available through The Nehru Archive; Hindustan Times, archival account of the 1 May 1960 inauguration, republished 4 May 2024.]

pictures.alt: The Act dated 25 April 1960 leads to Gujarat’s formation on 1 May 1960, its 132-member Assembly, separate High Court and first Chief Minister.
pictures.caption: A parliamentary law established the new state's territory and institutions.

title: The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 and the Birth of Gujarat's Institutions

body:
Ahmedabad as the first capital

When Gujarat was formed on 1 May 1960, Ahmedabad served as its capital. It retained this role from 1960 to 1970.

Ahmedabad was already a major commercial, industrial and educational centre. It had played an important role in India's freedom movement and was associated with Mahatma Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram. The initial choice of Ahmedabad therefore placed the new state administration in an established urban centre.

The shift to Gandhinagar

The state capital was shifted to Gandhinagar in 1970. Gandhinagar developed as a planned administrative city and became the seat of the state government's principal institutions.

The change of capital was an administrative relocation. It did not create a new state, change Gujarat's formation date or transfer its territory to another state.

Capital, commercial centre and High Court are different

A capital is the city designated as the seat of government. A state's largest commercial centre need not be its capital. Likewise, the principal seat of its High Court need not be located in the capital.

This distinction is particularly useful in Gujarat. Gandhinagar is the state capital, while Ahmedabad remains a major commercial centre and the seat of the Gujarat High Court. The Gujarat High Court was established in Ahmedabad in 1960 and continued to function there after the capital shifted.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat's first capital was Ahmedabad.
  • Ahmedabad served as capital from 1960 to 1970.
  • Gandhinagar became the capital in 1970.
  • The Gujarat High Court was established in Ahmedabad in 1960.
  • Trap: Gandhinagar is the capital, but the Gujarat High Court is located in Ahmedabad.

[Ahmedabad District Administration, Government of Gujarat, 'History,' paragraphs on Ahmedabad as capital from 1960 to 1970 and the subsequent shift to Gandhinagar, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat High Court, official 'About Gujarat High Court' page, sections on establishment and location, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Builders and engineers work beside newly constructed government buildings in Gandhinagar around 1970, with bamboo scaffolding and a period car.
Gujarat's capital shifted from Ahmedabad to Gandhinagar in 1970, while its High Court remained in Ahmedabad, where it was established on 1 May 1960.
pictures.caption: Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar have different administrative roles.
